topic: The Brachistochrone Problem: The Race of Curves

sections.title: The Hook: Which Path is Fastest?
sections.content: Introduce the challenge: A bead slides down a wire from point A to point B under gravity. Compare three paths: a straight line, a circular arc, and a 'mystery curve.' Frame it as a race where intuition often fails.
sections.example: Visualize a marble rolling down a slope. Most students guess the straight line is fastest; reveal that the actual solution is a curve that dips lower.

sections.title: Prerequisites: Conservation of Energy
sections.content: Briefly review the Work-Energy Theorem. Establish that velocity v = sqrt(2gh) at any vertical distance h. Explain that the time to descend is the integral of distance over speed.
sections.example: A diagram showing a particle's potential energy converting to kinetic energy as it descends along an arbitrary curve.

sections.title: The Calculus of Variations
sections.content: Introduce the concept of a 'functional'—optimizing the path itself rather than a single variable. Define the time integral equation T = ∫[1/v] ds, where ds is the arc length element.
sections.example: Animation showing the path changing shape (morphing) while the total time T is updated dynamically on a digital counter.

sections.title: The Solution: The Cycloid
sections.content: Present the Brachistochrone as a 'Cycloid'—the path traced by a point on the rim of a rolling circle. Explain that this shape balances distance vs. speed perfectly.
sections.example: An animation of a wheel rolling along a ceiling; a red dot on the rim traces the exact curve required to minimize travel time.

sections.title: Real-World Synthesis
sections.content: Conclude with applications of this principle, including the 'Tautochrone' property (why a clock's pendulum swings evenly) and how birds of prey use optimal descent trajectories.
sections.example: Show a Peregrine Falcon diving toward its prey; the falcon adjusts its flight angle to a near-cycloid path to maximize speed and accuracy.
